newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Central banks need European perspective - Duisenberg.
newsitem.headline: Central banks need European perspective - Duisenberg.

text.p: Dutch central bank president Wim Duisenberg said on Tuesday that European central banks must abandon national outlooks in favour of a European perspective if future decisions on monetary policy are to be effective.

Speaking in Washington, he told the spring membership meeting of the Institute of International Finance that national central banks would have more votes on the council of the planned European System of Central Banks (ESCB) than members of the European Central Bank (ECB) executive board.

The ESCB will consist of the ECB executive board, which is responsible for day-to-day monetary policy, the council, which is made up of the executive board and governors of the national central banks, and the national central banks themselves.
Duisenberg said the ESCB would have a federal structure comparable to the Federal Reserve system of the United States.

But national central bank governors would hold most of the votes, unlike the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) of the Federal Reserve Board, where the executive board of governors has a majority of the votes.

"This means that if effective decisions are to be arrived at in Europe, the national central bank governors will have to be like-minded; in other words, policy-makers will have to abandon their purely national outlooks, exchanging them for a 'European perspective'," Duisenberg said in his speech, a copy of which was made available by the Dutch central bank in Amsterdam.
"The experience of the FOMC shows that this can be achieved," he said.
The ESCB will be set up by the summer of 1998, ahead of the planned launch of European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.

Duisenberg takes over on July 1 as head of the European Monetary Institute and is seen as a strong candidate to be the first president of the ECB, which will oversee the planned launch of the single European currency in January 1999.
He said although the stability-oriented tradition which had grown up over the years would continue within EMU, there would be a fundamental change in the way monetary policy was conducted in Europe.
Contrary to present-day practice, policy would be determined centrally.

Duisenberg said there was no unequivocal answer to the question of how monetary policy could be best conducted, adding that it related to issues such as the economic variables on which policy should focus. "A decision is to be taken by the ECB on this point next year," he said.
But he said the Fed operated a well-balanced model of monetary decision-making, with policy conducted centrally and the interests of separate regions not overlooked.
"As in the U.S., policy in Europe will be determined centrally and implemented, where possible and appropriate, decentrally," Duisenberg said.
There were considerable similarities between this structure and the structure of the Fed, which is made up of the board of governors, FOMC and the reserve banks.
